column3: It nearly repeats the focus: taking devils as allies leads people to think they are guided while astray.
It adds Satanic prompting as a trial that exploits diseased and hardened hearts.
It directly portrays people blocking God's path and seeking to make it crooked.
It gives the parallel error of lost effort accompanied by confidence that one's work is good.
The immediately preceding ayah supplies the assigned satanic companion behind the focus's plural claim.
Its punishment image does not clarify obstruction from the path or mistaken guidance.
Satan beautifies deeds, blocks the path, and leaves its followers unguided.
The immediate sequel shows the eventual regret over that same evil companion.
It shows guidance refused after faith and clear proof, a distinct culpable route into misguidance.
It supplies a positive test case: following guides who seek no payment and are rightly guided.
It links disbelief in the Hereafter with beautified deeds and blind wandering.
Its general description of revelation as guidance adds little after more concrete path texts.
It extends false self-assessment to the Day of Resurrection, where their supposed standing is exposed.
The immediate continuation names manifest misguidance and the limits of guiding those closed to hearing.
It corrects a mistaken inference from delayed judgment, only indirectly related to mistaken guidance.
Its truth-versus-lie contrast offers only a broad epistemic boundary for the focus.
The affirmation of the Lord's cosmic rule gives a distant authority frame, not the focus's mechanism.
It corrects doubt about divine promise rather than the self-deception central to the focus.
It adds that beautified works can block the path even when people possess insight and visible evidence.
It gives the passage's positive counter-command: hold fast to revelation and the straight path.
Its mistaken appearance concerns sleepers, not persons misjudging their own direction.
It only states that the path was made easy, without addressing blockage or false guidance.
God's continual activity does not materially illuminate the focus's deception and path-blocking.
It identifies refusal to expect reckoning as a posture underlying the focus's false confidence.
It contrasts the focus's false claim with guidance joined to secure faith unmingled with wrong.
The immediate context adds that this revelation brings a coming accountability.
It presents hypocrisy using oaths as cover while actively blocking God's path.
Meeting the Lord and returning to Him supplies a close corrective to self-assured but misdirected conduct.
It gives the consequence of divine misguidance: no protector and no route of return.
It shows proud refusal of the invitation to forgiveness as enacted turning away.
The statement of Pharaoh's irritation has no useful connection to the focus.
The Lordship of east and west is a broad theological frame only.
The question about the cave companions does not add to the focus's moral miscalculation.
Its charge of lying is only a general contrast to the focus's false estimate.
Pharaoh explicitly claims to guide to right conduct, illustrating counterfeit guidance by an authority.
It directly warns against being turned from God's signs and pairs that warning with calling to the Lord.
Earlier in the same passage, ancestral imitation is explicitly called being guided, exposing the focus's inherited self-deception.
It associates divine non-guidance with excess and lying, but not the focus's pathway mechanism.
Its statement that God does not guide the defiantly corrupt adds a general consequence only.
A fearful military miscalculation is a remote instance of false estimation.
The two easts and wests echo later wording but do not clarify the focus itself.
Its division between guided and corrupt descendants is too general after earlier contrasts.
Mortality alone does not add to obstruction from the path or apparent guidance.
It models a sound response to a false report, a limited epistemic counterpoint.
It joins selling God's signs cheaply with blocking His way, giving a transactional motive.
Pharaoh's beautified evil and blockage from the path reinforce the counterfeit-guidance example.
The mirage sharply depicts a confident expectation collapsing into divine accounting.
It rebukes assuming that servants can be taken as protectors, a limited parallel to false reliance.
It combines accountability for every soul with beautified plotting and blockage from the path.
Its correction of an assumption about harm and good is not specifically about guidance.
Clear signs and God's guidance provide a concise positive counterpoint to the focus's delusion.
It joins obstructing God's path with resisting the messenger after guidance became clear.
It frames misguidance as leaving no protector and no possible way back when punishment is seen.
It identifies the Quran as guiding to what is most upright, the positive alternative to the focus.
The irrevocable arrival of punishment gives only a distant consequence for persistent deviation.
The oath by Sinai has no material connection to the focus.
It presents divine guidance as movement from darkness to light and onto a straight path.
Divine accounting gives an eschatological check on the focus's mistaken self-assessment.
It explicitly condemns treating an uninformed utterance as insignificant when it is grave before God.
In the same passage, it directly warns that Satan must not obstruct the audience.
Exclusion from hearing does not sufficiently specify the focus's self-deception.
The punishment detail adds nothing to the focus's path and guidance theme.
Its hoped-for guidance describes faithful worshippers but is redundant with earlier positive portraits.
Persecution for faith in God does not clarify the focus's claim to being guided.
The challenge to expecting easy entry into Paradise is only a broad correction of expectation.
The command to turn away and wait does not illuminate the focus.
Moses's trust that his Lord will guide him offers a concrete positive alternative to false self-guidance.
It explicitly joins preferring worldly life, blocking God's path, seeking its crookedness, and far misguidance.
Turning away from the message and punishment supply a general consequence only.
This later passage statement attributes their suffering to their own wrongdoing, not directly to misguidance.
Their paranoid assumption adds another kind of distorted self-assessment, but not a path reading.
The account of an impassable barrier is unrelated to moral obstruction from the path.
It locates genuine guidance to faith in God's favor rather than in a person's self-congratulation.
It repeats the core pattern of blocking God's path, seeking crookedness, and denying the Hereafter.
The claim that they will be guided concerns a local request and adds little here.
It is effectively redundant with the earlier, stronger formulation in 11:19.
It directly rejects the idea that people will not return to God, countering a root of false orientation.
It warns that following the majority can divert one from God's path through conjecture.
It identifies desire without divine guidance as a source of being led astray.
It describes an attempted misguidance that ultimately rebounds on its authors.
Following desires without knowledge is relevant but substantially covered by the prior desire-and-guidance text.
The praise of chosen righteous people has no clear marginal connection to the focus.
The Creator's continuing guidance is a broad positive contrast, already well represented.
It gives the costly outcome for those funding obstruction of God's path, after many direct examples.
It contrasts God's knowledge of who strays from His path with human knowledge narrowed by worldly aims.
Their lying claim to the best reward is a limited instance of self-deception.
Within the surah's ancestry discussion, it names the Creator as the one who will guide, but remains general.
It restates that disbelievers who block God's path have their deeds lost.
Its general guidance and mercy for the certain adds little after more specific corrective texts.
It warns against desires inherited from people who went astray and led many astray.
The bare notice of a false statement adds no useful detail to the focus.
It presents divine guidance as part of ordered creation, a broad positive frame only.
It tests a claim of being better guided against the actual arrival of clear proof and its rejection.
A community guiding by truth offers a general social contrast to the focus's misplaced guidance.
It attributes guidance to God and warns that association nullifies deeds, without a specific focus bridge.
It makes guidance to the Lord the route to reverent fear, a concrete positive endpoint.
God's true speech guiding the path supplies a broad contrast to human assertions.
The book as guidance and exclusive reliance on God is a general corrective only.
It records a baseless worldly-life theory and explicit conjecture, a close background to confident error.
The gift of scripture for guidance is general and already represented by more direct path passages.
Satan's declared ambush upon the straight path supplies the direct agency behind turning people from it.
It expands that ambush from every direction, explaining how gratitude and orientation are eroded.
One who abandons divine signs is followed by Satan and becomes among the straying.
Following desire instead of divine signs shows a human susceptibility that Satanic misdirection can exploit.
It distinguishes those God guides from those who are truly lost, directly testing a person's claim to guidance.
Satan vows to beautify worldly things and lead people astray, matching the focus's deceptive mechanism.
It sets the boundary that Satan has no authority over God's sincere servants.
It explicitly says Satan beautified earlier peoples' deeds, providing a historical parallel to the focus.
Satan's call, pressure, and promises describe active means of drawing people away from right direction.
It again limits Satan's authority over God's servants, clarifying that the focus's diversion is not irresistible.
Satan's whisper to Adam gives a concrete instance of seductive counsel that redirects judgment.
The wrong companion is said to have led a person away from the Reminder after it came to him.
It identifies those upon whom devils descend, adding a channel through which misleading speech is received.
Following inherited custom is contrasted with Satan's call, closely paralleling the surrounding 43:22-23 argument.
It explicitly names Satan as an enemy whose party he calls toward the Blaze.
Having an evil deed made fair so that one sees it as good closely matches the focus's false self-assessment.
The covenant not to worship Satan names him as an open enemy and gives the focus's allegiance contrast.
A constricted heart toward God's remembrance contrasts with the receptivity absent in the focus's setting.
After guidance becomes clear, Satan's enticement and false hopes explain a deliberate turning back.
Satan's domination makes people forget God's remembrance, a close antecedent to the companion assigned in 43:36.
Satan's promise followed by disavowal exposes the betrayal inherent in following his counsel.
